JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

Plaintiff and Intervenant, the
mother and father of Anthony Griffin ("Anthony"), are suing
Defendants under Arts 1053, 1054 and 1056 C.C. for the compensatory damages
suffered by them when Anthony. a black nineteen-year-old youth, was shot and
killed on November 11, 1987 in the parking lot of police Station 15 in Montréal by police officer Defendant
Allan Gosset ("Constable Gosset"). They are also claiming from
Defendants exemplary damages under
s. 49
of the
Québec Charter of Human
Rights and Freedoms
(
[1]
)
(the "Québec Charter").

FACTS

a.
Events Leading up to Parking
lot Scene

Around 5:20 a.m. on November 11,
1987 taxi driver Normand Leduc ("Mr. Leduc") picked up Anthony at a
Dunkin Donuts restaurant at 5821 Côte des Neiges. They then drove along Gatineau Street while Anthony tried to
locate a particular residence. When he ordered Mr. Leduc to stop, Anthony got
out, went over behind some bushes and under a gallery and brought back to the
taxi a green polyethylene garbage bag which he placed in the taxi between the
front and back seats. Anthony then ordered Mr. Leduc to drive him to the South
Seas restaurant on St-Jacques Street.

Upon arrival, Anthony advised Mr.
Leduc that he had no money to pay the fare but that the manager of the
restaurant would pay for him when he arrived. Some twenty minutes later the
manager arrived but refused to pay Anthony's taxi fare. Mr. Leduc then told
Anthony he was going to call the police. Anthony pleaded with him not to do so
saying that he had a wife and two children whom he would not be able to see if
he was put in prison over the Christmas holidays. Mr. Leduc called the police.
Anthony and Mr. Leduc remained seated in the taxi awaiting the arrival of the
police. At approximately 6:30 a.m. Constable Gosset, an officer of some 14
years experience with Defendant Montreal Urban Community ("MUG"), and
his partner, Kimberley Campbell ("Constable Campbell"), with only 2
months experience, were dispatched in car 15-2 to answer Mr. Leduc's call.

When Constables Gosset and Campbell
arrived at the South Seas
restaurant, Anthony got out of the taxi and walked over to talk to them. After
some discussion, Mr. Leduc advised Constable Gosset that he did not wish to go
to the trouble of laying a charge against Anthony.

Constable Gosset asked Anthony for
his name and birth date. Anthony gave his name as "Tony Bowers".
Constable Gosset and Anthony then got into the patrol car and Constable Gosset
used the car radio to check with the central data bank. He was advised that
Tony Bowers was white.

Constable Gosset then asked Anthony
to get out of the patrol car so he could check his pockets for identification.
Anthony got out of the car and Constable Gosset, while standing in front of
Anthony, searched his pockets. He found a letter addressed to a certain
"Anthony Griffin". Constable Gosset and Anthony got back into the
patrol car. Anthony in the back and Constable Gosset in the passenger seat. He
again checked with the central data bank and found that Anthony was wanted on a
bench warrant. Constable Gosset then arrested Anthony and advised him of his
rights.

Mr. Leduc testified that while
waiting for the police in the taxi Anthony had never attempted to run away or
to threaten him. Mr. Leduc also confirmed that during the whole incident in
front of the South Seas restaurant, there was no shouting, shoving or violence
of any kind. Both Constable Gosset and Anthony were calm and polite with each
other. Anthony cooperated with all requests made of him by Constable Gosset
except that he refused to give his correct name. At no time did Constable
Gosset place handcuffs on Anthony.

As Constables Gosset and Campbell
were about to drive off to Station 15, Mr. Leduc suddenly remembered the green
garbage bag in his taxi and handed it to Constable Campbell. It contained a
considerable number of packages of cigarettes of different brands. At about
7:00 a.m. Mr. Leduc left to pick up a fare in another part of the city.
Constable Campbell drove patrol car 15-2, with Constable Gosset and Anthony in
it, directly to the Station 15 parking lot. The trip took about 5 to 7 minutes.

b.
Events in Station 15 Parking
lot

Just after 7:00 a.m. Constable
Campbell parked the patrol car facing the Station and approximately 25 feet from the back door. Constable
Gosset got out of the passenger seat and opened the back right door. Anthony
stepped out, closed the door, took two or three steps and started running in
front of the car towards Station 15. Constable Gosset started to run after him
while Constable Campbell stood a few feet from the car door on the driver's
side.

Because the events of the next few
seconds are extremely important, the Court cites at length relevant extracts
from the trial testimony of Constable Campbell :

May 4, 1990, p. 46 :

"Q        Tell the Court what
you heard ?

A          I heard Cosset yell -
"stop" - and then I heard him say - "stop" - again, and
then I heard him say - "stop or I'll shoot"."

and at p. 51 :

"Q        And when - would you
describe the movements of Mr. Griffin after you heard the first scream of
-"stop"- ?

A          Mr. Griffin did stop and
he turned around to face Mr. Cosset, and he stood there with his legs spread
and he had his arms on either side of his body raised slightly, and he was
dodging, he was putting his weight from one foot to the other."

May 7, 1990, p. 17 :

"Q        During the three (3)
seconds that elapsed between the time that Mr. Griffin was facing Mr. Cosset,
and the time the shot went off, did you see the revolver in the hands of Mr.
Cosset ?

A          Yes, when Mr. Gosset
stopped and turned his back towards me. I could see the gun in his right hand.

Q         And at all times, he only
had one hand on the revolver ?

A          That's correct.

Q         And, at a certain moment,
he pointed the revolver at Mr. Griffin ?

A          I saw him lift his, his right
arm in a. in a straight - he kept his arm straight and he lifted it like that.

Q         And, as he lifted the arm,
did the revolver end up being pointed at the suspect ?

A          The gun never stopped
its, its motion, it kept going. It never stopped, he never hesitated.

Q         About how much time
elapsed from the time that it first was pointing to the ground, am I correct in
saying, prior to being lifted it ... (interrupted)

A          Right.

Q         ... (continued) -- it was
pointed-the revolver was pointed towards the ground ?

A          Yes.

Q         To the time when the shot
went off ?

A          "Time"., maybe
a second."

and at pp. 60 and 61 :

"Q        And, it's your
testimony that at the time you saw him with the gun, first it was pointed
towards the ground ?

A          That's correct.

Q         How long the gun remained
pointed towards the ground ?

A          I don't remember. maybe a
second, maybe two, not very long.

Q         Isn't it true that
actually the time you watched him, you saw the gun being lifted from the ground
towards Mr. Griffin ?

A          I saw him lift it, yes.

Q         Okay. - But, you did not
see the gun remaining pointed towards the ground, for a certain period of the
time ?

A          Well, when he turned -
when he turned around. I believe that's when he said - "stop" - for
the second time. and the gun was still pointing down, he must have kept it
there for about a second. enough to say something.

Q         Okay. - I understand it's
your testimony that Mr. Gosset first said - "stop" - and Mr. Griffin
did actually stop ?

A          Yes, he did."

and at p. 62 :

"Q        And the third time -
"stop I'll shoot." - what was the gun(?) position when      you heard
this ‑ "stop or I'll shoot" ?

A          He lifted it right at the
end, right after he said - "stop or I'll shoot" - he just lifted it
and it went off and it just kept going, it never, it never stopped
anywhere."

and at pp. 105 and 106 :

"Q        Do you remember in
the context of the "stop, stop, stop or I'll shoot" that he stopped
after the first. he called out "stop. Mr.
Griffin
", when did he turn around ?

A          He turned around at the
same time,

Q         At the same time as before
the second "stop" had been called out ?

A          That's right, the first
time that Mr. Gosset said "stop", Griffin did stop and he turned
around right afterwards.

Q         And, therefore, it was
when Mr. Griffin was facing Constable Gosset when Constable Cosset called out
the second "stop", is that correct ?

A          That's correct.

Q         And, presumably also when
he said-"stop or I'll shoot" - Mr. Griffin was still facing Constable
Gosset ?

A          That's right. "

The Court has no reason to doubt the
veracity of Constable Campbell's testimony. In the witness box, her replies
were clear and concise and she did not hesitate to admit when she did not
remember something. She had only been a police officer for approximately two
months at the time of the November 11th incident. Because this was a new experience
for her, the Court is of the opinion that her memory is probably quite accurate
under the circumstances.

Constable Campbell also testified
that for the few split seconds Anthony and Constable Gosset were facing each
other, she saw no gesture on the part of Anthony that she considered dangerous
for Constable Gosset.

In his October 19, 1989 deposition,
Constable Gosset gave his explanation as to why he raised his revolver and
pointed it at Anthony :

At pp. 111 and 112 :

"Q        Pourquoi avez-vous
levé votre arme en direction d'Anthony Griffin ?

R         Afin de le contrôler à
distance et pour qu'il se soumette complètement à cette arrestation.

Q         Mais au moment que vous
levez l'arme dans la direction d'Anthony Griffin, étiez-vous en contrôle de
cette arme-là ?

R         Pour moi, oui.

Q         Est-ce que c'est exact de
dire que vous avez monté l'arme avec une main en pointant dans sa
direction ?

R         Oui."

Unfortunately, the events of the
next few seconds not have control of his revolver. The gun indicate quite
clearly that Constable Gosset did discharged and Anthony was shot through the
head Just above his right eye brow. He fell onto his back unconscious in the
parking lot. An ambulance arrived in a few minutes. He was driven to the Jewish
General Hospital where he expired 4 hours later without regaining
consciousness.

It was Constable Gosset who made the
decision to run after Anthony alone rather than to ask for assistance from his
partner. Constable Gosset admitted that he drew his revolver from its holster
as he was running. At no time did he feel that his life or the life of his
partner was in any danger. He also admitted that it was dangerous to run with a
revolver in his hand.

The event occurred in broad daylight
not more than 25 feet from the back door of Station 15. The parking lot surface
was paved and flat and there is no evidence that Constable Gosset stumbled or
tripped as he was running after Anthony.

PRELIMINARY COMMENTS

The Court does not intend to deal
specifically with each and every one of Plaintiff's numerous allegations. By
far the greater number of them were completely unsubstantiated by proper proof.
Many days of trial could have been avoided had Plaintiff's attorney followed
the basic evidentiary rules of (a) relevancy, (b) best evidence and (c)
hearsay.

During the trial, each of the four
attorneys objected on various occasions to elements of proof that they
considered irrelevant. The Court took these objections under reserve, These
objections are now dismissed.

The MUC has admitted its
responsibility for the compensatory damages to which Plaintiff and Intervenant
are entitled due to the death of their son. Only the amount remains to be
determined by the Court.

Plaintiff alleged that, following
the shooting, the MUC participated in an unlawful attempt to cover up the true
facts in order to protect Constable Cosset. The proof simply does not support
such an allegation. Constable Gosset admitted from the very beginning that he
shot Anthony but that he had not intended to do so. There was nothing left to
"cover up".

However, it was certainly
unfortunate that the subsequent investigation of the shooting was carried out
by the MUC police rather than by an independent police force. An inquiry by an
outside police force would have done much to allay the understandable suspicions
of Montreal's black community.

Plaintiff also alleged that
"there had been a grave travesty of justice in all respects"
involving the following judicial proceedings pertaining to Constable Gosset's
behaviour on November 11, 1987 :

1.         the Québec Police Commission
inquiry ;

2.         his trial for manslaughter before
the Superior Court, Criminal Division ;

3.         the arbitration hearing of the
grievance concerning his dismissal from the MUC police ; and

4.         the trial before the Superior
Court of the evocation proceedings taken by the MUC against the arbitrator's
decision to reinstate.

To say the least, this allegation is
most extraordinary ! However, the Court's role in the present case is not
to sit in appeal of the decisions rendered in these prior proceedings. Rather,
it must, based upon the proof presented to it in the present case, determine
the amount of compensatory damages to be awarded to Plaintiff and Intervenant
resulting from the death of their son and whether Constable Gosset is also
responsible for these damages. The Court must also decide whether either or
both of Constable Gosset and the MUC should be condemned to exemplary damages.

Because the present proceedings are
civil in nature, Defendants may be condemned on a mere balance of
probabilities. It is not necessary to establish responsibility beyond a
reasonable doubt.

ALLEGED RACIAL DISCRIMINATION

Plaintiff also alleged that
Constable Cosset was prejudiced against black citizens because he had committed
two acts of racial discrimination in the performance of his duties. One
allegedly occurred at the time of the shooting in the parking lot of Station 15
and was reported on Radio Station CKAC. The other allegedly took place during
the night of July 17, 1981 when he was attempting to arrest another black citizen,
Daniel Otchere.

a.
Broadcast by Radio Station
CKAC

The first act concerns the words
allegedly shouted by Constable Gosset to Constable Campbell as Anthony
attempted to flee : "Arrête...on court pas après un noir". These
words were then reported by a certain Richard Desmarais, a journalist
specializing in police matters, during a broadcast from Radio Station CKAC two
days after the shooting.

Both Constables Gosset and Campbell,
the only persons to witness the attempted flight of Anthony, categorically deny
that these words were ever uttered by Constable Gosset. In fact, the proof
indicates that the words were nothing but a vicious rumor repeated by a certain
Sergeant-Detective Rouleau, a 20-year veteran with the MUC (now retired) to Mr.
Desmarais at an oyster party the day after the shooting. Mr. Rouleau, who could
not remember either the source of the rumor or the context in which he had
heard it, stated in his May 10, 1990 testimony :

"... Moi, j'ai répété, j'ai
dit ça à Monsieur Desmarais, en lui précisant que c'était une rumeur que
j'avais entendue dans l'édifice du poste numéro trente-trois (33) où, à
l'endroit où je travaillais.

(...)

Je me souviens que Monsieur
Desmarais a paru très très intéressé par ce que je lui disais, alors, ce qui
m'a fait..., ce qui m'a fait le cautionner à l'effet que ce n'était qu'une
rumeur, que c'était pas pour publication, qu'il y avait rien de prouvé
là-dedans, c'était une rumeur de salle de garde.

(...)

Je ne faisais pas circuler une
rumeur, Votre Seigneurie, je lui déclarais la nature de la rumeur en lui
précisant que c'était une rumeur, qu'elle ne devait pas circuler, qu'elle
devait pas être pour publication. Il était cautionné très très soigneusement à
cet effet-là."

The following question from the
Court and Mr. Rouleau's answer are even more enlightening :

"Q        N'est-il pas vrai que
la meilleure façon d'éviter cette aggravation de la tension serait tout
simplement de ne pas la communiquer, point ?

R         C'est exact."

The repeating of this kind of
gratuitous venom, by an experienced police officer who should have known
better, to a member of the press at a cocktail party was most regrettable.
However, even more regrettable was the fact that Mr. Desmarais chose to
disseminate over the Montréal airwaves what he clearly knew to be a rumor.

The spoken and written press is an
indispensable and essential component of a free and democratic society. Indeed,
the
Québec Charter
specifically recognizes the importance of the press.

However, the deliberate spreading of
inflammatory statements, having no basis in fact, for the sole purpose of
sensationalizing a tragic event is not the sign of a healthy and responsible
press. Mr. Desmarais' actions in this matter only served to heighten a mother's
grief, to cause further prejudice toward a police officer and to exacerbate
unnecessarily the relationship between the black community and the MUC.

b.
The Otchere Incident

The Court watched Mr. Otchere as he
testified concerning the altercation on Clarke Street in 1981 and then reviewed the transcript of his testimony. The
Court is left with the distinct impression that Mr. Otchere would say or do
anything to "get" Constable Gosset for what happened the night of
July 17, 1981 when Constable Gosset was attempting to arrest him. His attitude
coupled with the lapse of almost nine years seem to have severely affected his
memory. Nor was the Court particularly impressed with the accuracy of the
testimony of Constable Monique Tremblay, Constable Gosset's partner that
particular night.

The Court is satisfied that Mr.
Otchere received a blow in the face from a police flashlight. However, the
ensuing mêlée was certainly provoked by Mr. Otchere's violent resistance to
arrest. At any event, in the opinion of the Court, the Otchere incident was not
sufficient to brand Constable Gosset as a brutal aggressor who regularly
discriminated against black citizens,

Finally, the Court does not doubt
that there are some racist individuals in the MUC police -- just as there are
in all segments of our society. However, in the opinion of the Court, Anthony's
death was not caused by an act of racial discrimination. Rather, it resulted
from an excessive and unjustified use of force by a police officer.

RESPONSIBILITY OF CONSTABLE GOSSET
UNDER ART.
1053 C
.C.

a.
Duties of Police Officers
Generally

The investigation of a crime and the
detection of criminals is not a game governed by the Marquis of Queensberry
rules. However, it is necessary to distinguish
the duties
of police
officers from
the powers
they possess to execute those duties. The fact
that a police officer has a general duty to prevent crime and protect life and
property does not mean that he can use any or all means for achieving these
ends. The police have wide duties but limited powers.

A police officer is not empowered to
execute his duty by unlawful means. The public interest in law enforcement
cannot be allowed to override the fundamental principle that all public
officials, including police officers, are subject to the rule of law. To find
that any police action is justified simply because it is directed at the
fulfillment of police duties, would be to sanction a dangerous exception to the
supremacy of law.

Police officers stand at the
forefront of the law and order processes of society. They restrain the
violator, protect the compliant and represent constituted authority in both the
peace and the turbulence of community life. The community depends heavily upon
their skill and availability. They deserve and require the understanding and
support of all citizens, including judges. Where any police officer fails -
whether for lack of courage, judgment, integrity or humaneness -- all the
community suffers. It suffers because vested authority has failed to prevent
some harm or because authority has been sullied and abused. With every abuse of
authority, the entire ordering process is weakened. The public truste the
entire process less and antagonism to all figures of authority rises. No one
should be more alert to the cost of failure than responsible law enforcement
officers and the judges who work in the courts.

Every effort must be made to avoid
the failures, to prevent their reoccurrence and, at all times, to stay true to
the requisites of honesty and accountability imposed upon all who are, at the
same time, representative of the law and subject to it.

Police officers, when acting or
purporting to act in their official capacity, only act lawfully if they act in
the exercise of authority which is either conferred by statute or derived as a
matter of common law. The authority of police officers is not unlimited. They
must know its limits and, if they disregard or ignore them, they commit a
fault.

As Boilard J. recently stated
(
[2]
)
:

"...Faut-il répéter encore
une fois que le policier exerce une profession difficile, exigeante et dangereuse.
Il doit connaître toutes les lois et leurs plus récentes modifications ;
il doit posséder un jugement inattaquable et faire montre de
discernement ; il doit enfin assumer de grands risques dans la poursuite
des criminels et leur arrestation."

b.
Use of Firearms by Police
Officers

The more dangerous an object is, the
higher is the duty of care required of those who handle it.. Loaded firearms
are extremely dangerous and the law requires consummate caution in every person
who handles them. The duty of care is so high that it borders on strict
liability. As the highly qualified American firearms expert, Massad Ayoob,
stated : "...by definition, its never safe to point a deadly weapon
at any human being, even if it's empty" (Exhibit DG-2). The inherent
danger of a loaded firearm dictates that it must never be handled carelessly or
pointed unnecessarily where it could cause damage if discharged.

5.86 of the
Criminal Code

acknowledges the extreme danger surrounding the handling of firearms when it
states,
inter alia
, that every one who,
without lawful excuse
,
(1) points a firearm at another person, whether the firearm is loaded or not,
or (2) uses, carries or handles any firearm in a careless manner or without
reasonable precautions for the safety of other persons, is guilty of an
offence.

The police must not resort to the
ultimate form of compulsion, the firearm, upon any appearance of resistance and
with only imagined justification. The firearm should not be a badge or
theatrical "prop" or the source of false courage. It should always be
regarded as a deadly and dangerous weapon. Whenever he resorts to his firearm,
the police officer is answerable to the law and must expect that his actions
will be closely scrutinized. The courts must not condone the careless handling
of firearms by police officers.

It should also be noted that any
abuse of authority, any intimidation or any recourse to unjustified force by an
MUC police officer is a professional breach of discipline
(
[3]
)
.

Although police officers in this country
are furnished with firearms, such firearms should only be used in very
exceptional circumstances. The framework respecting the liability of police
officers for damages done through the use of firearms in the course of duty is
found in
s. 25
of the
Criminal Code
which section provides, in part :

"25, (1) Every one who is
required or authorised by law to do anything in the administration or
enforcement of the law

(...)

(b) as a peace officer or public
officer,

(...)

is, if he acts on reasonable
grounds. justified in doing what he is required or authorized to do and
in
using as much force as necessary for that purpose
.

(...)

(3) Subject to subsection (4), a
person is not justified for the purposes of subsection (1) in using force that
is intended or is likely to cause death or grievous bodily harm
unless he
believes on reasonable grounds that it is necessary for the purpose of
preserving himself or any one under his protection from death or grievous
bodily harm
.

(4) A peace officer who is
proceeding lawfully to arrest, with or without warrant, any person for an
offence for which that person may be arrested without warrant... is justified,
if the person to be arrested takes flight to avoid arrest,
in using as much
force is necessary to prevent the escape by flight, unless the escape can be
prevented by reasonable means in a less violent manner
."

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

As Lamer J. stated in the Supreme
Court of Canada decision,
Roberge
v.
R.
(
[4]
)
:

"Under s. 25(1), the purpose
is to arrest, while under s. 25(4) the purpose is to prevent escape from
immediate arrest. As I have already said, this difference of purpose has a
direct bearing on the nature of the force the reasonableness of which is to be
assessed.

(...)

...Section 25(4) is a codification
of the old common law applicable to fleeing felons, offenders that would in
those days, if found guilty, most certainly be executed. Many suggestions have
been made to Parliament as regards this frightful arsenal peace officers enjoy
(see. amongst others, the Ouimet Committee Report). particularly concerning
offences that do not indicate dangerousness on the part of the offender, such
as shoplifting, fraud, gambling. We have extended to all indictable offences a
common law principle that was intended to be applied only to felons. This is a
choice Parliament has made and which the courts cannot defeat."

Where there is appropriate
justification,
s. 25
relieves the police officer of any civil or criminal
liability, not only in respect of the fugitive but also in respect of any
person who accidentally becomes an innocent victim of the force used by such
officer
(
[5]
)
.

However, where the right of a police
officer to use force exists, it must be exercised in a reasonable manner
(
[6]
)
. The reasonableness of the officer's
actions will be determined in relation to the particular circumstances of each
case.

As Tellier J. stated in
Carrière

v.
Cité de Longueuil
(
[7]
)
:

"La jurisprudence est constante à l'effet que, même dans les
cas d'arrestation ou de fuite des criminels, les agents de la paix et toute
personne requise de les assister, doivent
agir avec mesure et modération

et n'employer que la force et les moyens nécessités par les
circonstances."

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

However, the law does not require an
impossible degree of calmness and detachment. The officer's actions must be
judged with due regard for the stress and tension of the moment.

In
Béliveau
v.
Lafond
(
[8]
)
, involving a civil damage claim by a
suspect who was wounded by a police officer during an attempted arrest. Beauregard J. stated :

"Même si l'appelant était
justifié de mettre l'intimé sous arrêt, il ne devait pas, à cette fin, utiliser
plus que la force nécessaire dont parle l'article 25 (4) C.Cr.

La charge de la preuve à ce sujet incombait à l'appelant
et celui-ci n'a pas fait la preuve qu'il n'aurait pas pu faire
l'arrestation autrement qu'en tirant au moins deux fois vers la chaloupe.
L'appelant n'avait pas d'informations lui laissant croire que les individus
étaient armés ou qu'ils etaient dangereux ou qu'ils avaient commis un acte
tellement grave que cela le justifiait de mettre sous arrêt ces personnes même
au prix de blessures graves...
"

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

S. 25 (4) should be strictly
construed and should not provide an "out" in cases where there is a
basis for saying that escape could have been prevented by reasonable means in a
less violent manner
(
[9]
)
. Where a suspect poses no serious threat either to the police
officer or to others. the harm resulting from failing to apprehend him on the
spot dues not justify resorting to a firearm. The value of human life should be
placed above the necessity to effect immediate arrest.

As Toth J. stated in
Charrette

v.
Dorais
(
[10]
)
:

"... le défendeur, en tirant le coup de fusil, a attenté à la
vie du demandeur. La vie est ce qu'il y a de plus précieux que l'homme possède
et tout système juridique l'entoure de protection et oblige toute personne à la
respecter.
Même le criminel a droit à sa vie et ce n'est qu'en des cas
extrêmes que la loi autorise d'y attenter
...".

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

Was the immediate apprehension of
Anthony in the parking lot of Station 15 of such paramount importance that his
life and the lives of innocent third parties were to be risked ? The Court
thinks not.

c.
Testimony of Firearms
Experts

Witness Gravel, the person in the
police scientific laboratory of the Ministère du Solliciteur général who
examined Constable Gosset's revolver following the shooting, testified that it
was in proper firing condition and that only 1,3 kg of force on the trigger was
required to cause it to fire when in single action mode, i.e., when the hammer
was cocked. He was also of the opinion that a trigger movement of approximately
4/1,000 of an inch was all that was required for it to fire. Finally, witness
Gravel confirmed the obvious, i.e., a revolver does not fire by itself !

Witness Ménard, an MUC firearms
instructor for 7½ years, testified that, when drawing a Smith & Wesson 38
from its holster, a police officer could unconsciously cock the hammer of the
revolver, i.e., place it in single action mode. He explained that this could
happen in one of three ways : because the seat belt in the patrol car had
accidentally caused the hammer to cock ; because a worn or loose strap on
the holster had caused it to happen ; or because "reflex action"
caused the officer (originally trained in the manner that Constable Gosset was
prior to 1979) to cock the hammer automatically as he withdrew the revolver
from its holster. Witness Ménard advised that these risks were explained to all
MUC police officers when they received their firearms instruction.

Witness Ménard also stated that. for
a person experienced in the handling of small arms, if the recoil from the shot
caused the arm holding the revolver to jump upwards, this was one sign that the
person was not expecting the gun to fire at that moment. He also confirmed
that, in single action mode, a Smith & Wesson 38 was extremely delicate and
extremely dangerous. Finally, he demonstrated the correct method for firing the
revolver, i.e., by holding it with both hands and with arms fully extended in
front of the body at 90°.

The following extract from the
testimony of American firearms expert Massad Ayoob, given before the Québec
Police Commission on May 4, 1988 (filed as Exhibit DG-2 in the present case), is extremely
enlightening (despite the obvious problems of the court stenographer when
transcribing the testimony !) :

"Now, we're talking about
here would be a movement was sort of a pendulum effect, if you will. If we have
the revolver, the Smith and Wesson in question is in respect for a weight of
thirty and one half (30½) onces when it's unloaded. We have that plus the
weight of the six (6) live cartridges in the firing chamber. Now, if one had
been running forward with the gun in their hands, the gun is maintaining a
fairly constant relationship in that hand however loose it might be. Now, as
the gun comes up suddenly, as the gun is thrown forward towards the loose
finger as the gun hits ; we literally had a case of the trigger hitting
the finger instead of the finger hitting the trigger and the gun at that point
could fire.

What convinces me that this is
probably what did happen, is the universal description of the violent recoil of
the revolver. The
Montreal
issue load, issued cartridge is a thirty-eight (38) special, one
forty (140) grains soft nose bullet loaded to plus B velocity. Recoils or kicks
somewhat more than a convention thirty-eight. (38) caliber round and held
firmly by a man of Constable Gusset's size, one would see probably the recoil
that I'll attempt to demonstrate for you now with the empty gun, one would see
a snap and then the gun coming hack on target with the body weight behind it.
We find however if the gun is held loosely, and the gun is allowed to recoil by
itself, you will see the violent lift of the gun with the arm falling. Now that
is absolutely consistent with the gun being held loosely, it was not at all be
consistent with the gun being fired intentionally by anyone who had ever fired
such a gun before knowing the type of recoil that. they would be dealing
with."

d.
Constable Gosset's Use of
his Revolver

The Court simply does not believe
that Constable Gosset drew and pointed his revolver because he thought Anthony
might be armed. He had already searched at least three of Anthony's pockets
when looking for identification papers and had found no weapon. In the parking
lot, Anthony's hands were visible at all times and he had nothing in them, nor
did he make any gesture that threatened Constable Gosset.

This is not a case where a police
officer was chasing a known and dangerous criminal down a dark alleyway at
night, or where a police officer has been called to the scene of a
hostage-taking by an armed man, or where an officer was attempting to control a
crazed drug addict. In these types of situations, it may be absolutely
necessary for the officer to draw, aim and even fire in order to defend himself
or to protect innocent persons.

It is extremely important to note
that Anthony stopped fleeing and turned around upon Constable Gosset's first
order to stop. It was not the sight of the revolver that caused Anthony to stop
because his back was towards Constable Cosset who had not yet threatened to
shoot. At this point, Anthony was no longer attempting to escape arrest and, in
the opinion of the Court, Constable Gosset was no longer Justified in resorting
to his revolver.

Constable Gosset was negligent when
he drew his revolver while running and again when he pointed it at Anthony at
extremely close range with his finger on the trigger. Constable Gosset knew (or
should have known) from his firearms training and previous experience that his
revolver might well be in single action mode with a "hair trigger. He
offered no explanation for how the gun discharged other than to say it was an
accident, This negligence was a direct cause of Anthony's death. The use of
this amount of force was totally unnecessary and unjustified. Therefore,
Constable Gosset is responsible for the damages caused in virtue of Art. 1053
C.C.

CONSTABLE GOSSET'S ACTIONS AND S. 49
OF
QUEBEC
CHARTER

S. 49
of the
Québec Charter
(which
section came into effect June 28, 1976) provides that :

"Any unlawful interference
with any right or freedom recognized by this Charier entitles the victim to
obtain the cessation of such interference and compensation for the moral or
material prejudice resulting therefrom.

In case of unlawful and intentional interference, the tribunal may,
in addition, condemn the person guilty of it to exemplary damages
."

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

It is now necessary to determine
whether Constable Gosset's actions amounted to an unlawful and intentional
interference" ("atteinte illicite et intentionnelle") with
Anthony's rights the
Québec Charter
.
S. 1
states, in part :

"Every human being has a
right to personal security, inviolability and freedom."

The right to personal security and
inviolability ...comprend le droit de toute personne de se protéger et d'être
protégée contre ce qui pourrait menacer son intégrité"
(
[11]
)
.
The "right to personal security" must
encompass freedom from the
threat
of physical attack as well as freedom
from such attack itself. The Court has difficulty imagining what could be more
threatening to one's personal security than looking down the muzzle of a loaded
Smith & Wesson 38 with someone else's finger on the trigger !

The Court has no doubt that once
Anthony had stopped fleeing the level of force Constable Gosset was attempting
to use in order to get Anthony from the parking lot into Station 15 was
completely unnecessary and unjustified, and therefore unlawful.

Were his actions
"intentional" ? One must try and put oneself in Constable
Gosset's position and try to imagine what was going through his mind. Through
good routine police work, he had arrested a person wanted on a bench warrant
and who was also apparently in possession of stolen goods. While he and his
partner were driving Anthony to Station 15, he had announced over the police
radio or walkie-talkie : "On a pogné le jack pot" ! He was
within 25 feet of the back door
of Station 15 with his suspect when suddenly his "jack pot" seemed to
be slipping through his fingers ! Even worse, his partner, a rookie police
officer of less than two months experience, was watching the whole episode a
few feet away. What would his colleagues say if he had to enter the Station
empty-handed to explain that his suspect had just escaped in the Station's
parking lot !

The proof indicates that Constable
Gosset chose consciously and deliberately to run after Anthony without
requesting assistance. He consciously and deliberately pulled his revolver from
its holster as he was running, He consciously and deliberately shouted at
Anthony to stop while running with his revolver in one hand. After Anthony had
stopped running, turned around to face him and was shifting his weight from
foot to foot, he consciously and deliberately again ordered him to stop. He
consciously and deliberately, when there were no more than 20 feet between
them, raised his revolver in one hand with his finger on the trigger while at
the same time shouting "Stop or I'll shoot".

The Court is satisfied that
Constable Gosset did not actually intend to fire the shot that struck Anthony
in the forehead and killed him. However, the fact that these conscious and
deliberate acts, which were both reckless and unlawful, had a result which
Constable Gosset did not intend surely does not, if that result was one which
he ought reasonably to have anticipated, entitle him to claim that it was an
accident.

As Chevalier J. stated in
West
Island Teachers' Association
v.
Nantel
(
[12]
)
, a case involving exemplary damages
due to infringement of rights under
ss. 1
,
3
,
4
and
5
of the
Québec
Charter
:

"On ne saurait créer un état
de choses aussi potentiellement générateur de troubles et ensuite se retrancher
derrière l'excuse qu'on n'en a jamais voulu les suites, dont on sait fort bien
que, presque inéluctablement, elles se produiraient..."

The basic concepts of fault and
negligence are well understood and readily recognized by most members of
society. However, the way that one characterizes
the degree
of fault or
negligence in any given fact situation is not so well known. Fault and
negligence are a continuum. One starts at one end with the conduct of the
reasonable man (perhaps a reasonable person in today's context) and progresses
(or rather regresses) to criminal conduct at the other end. In civil law, it is
the domain of the judge to decide exactly where in the continuum the conduct of
a particular defendant should be located and this he does in the only way
possible, i.e., by using words to characterize the degree of fault.

In Québec, jurists start at one end
of the continuum by such words as simple negligence or "faute légère".
They then move along the continuum to gross negligence ("faute lourde"),
to wanton or reckless misconduct ("faute lourde dolosive"), to
intentional fault ("faute intentionnelle" ou "délit") and
finally reaching the other end where one finds criminal negligence ("acte
criminel").

In a civil action for compensatory
damages, if it is proved that a person falls short of the standard of
reasonable care required by law, it matters not how far such a person fell
short of that standard. The extent of his liability depends not on the degree
of negligence but on the amount of damage done. However, in a criminal court or
in a civil court considering a claim for exemplary damages, the amount and the
degree of negligence are extremely relevant.

If the conduct of the defendant is
no worse than that it simply does not measure up to the conduct of a reasonable
person, he can be condemned to damages under Art, 1053 C.C. If the defendant's conduct is
found to be criminal negligence, he can be imprisoned for up to ten years. The
two ends of the continuum are easy to find but locating conduct in between is
considerably more difficult.

How should one interpret the phrase
"intentional interference" ("atteinte intentionnelle"), as
this phrase is used in the second paragraph of
s. 49
of the
Québec
Charter
? Three eminent Québec jurists have recently considered this
point. Baudoin J. states
(
[13]
)
:

"... Encore faut-il cependant que l'atteinte ait été
intentionnelle. L'emploi de l'adjectif "intentionnelle" par le
législateur me semble indiquer qu'il ne veut pas se contenter simplement d'une
faute lourde, mais qu'il exige, au contraire, de démontrer
le caractère
voulu, conscient, délibéré de l'acte posé
...".

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

Professor Rousseau-Houle J. (as she
then was) states
(
[14]
)
:

"... la
Charte
donne un recoure complémentaire lorsqu'il y a
atteinte intentionnelle et illicite à la réputation ou aux biens. La preuve de
la faute intentionnelle ou du moins de
la négligence inexcusable
est
exigée...".

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

Chevalier J. states
(
[15]
)
:

..Pour être intentionnel, il faut qu'il soit commis dans des
circonstances qui indiquent une volonté déterminée de causer le dommage
résultant de la violation. Cette volonté peut se manifester de plusieurs
façons. Elle est susceptible d'apparaître par suite de la constatation que la
faute commise est lourde ou grossière au point que l'esprit ne saurait
s'imaginer que celui qui l'a commise ne pouvait pas ne pas se rendre compte au
départ qu'elle produirait les conséquences préjudiciables qui en ont été la
suite. La faute est également intentionnelle si elle provient d'
une
insouciance déréglée et téméraire du respect du droit d'autrui, en parfaite
connaissance des conséquences, immédiates et naturelle, ou au moins extrêmement
probables que, son geste va causer à sa victime
."

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

One of the more enlightened comments
concerning the degree of fault necessary for "intentional
interference" under
s. 49
is that of Professor Louis Perret
(
[16]
)
:

"Qu'est ce qu'une faute
intentionnelle ? La question n'a jamais été tellement approfondie en
responsabilité civile, du fait que traditionnellement elle n'avait pas
d'incidence particulière sur l'indemnisation. Cette notion a cependant été
analysée en jurisprudence dans le domaine des assurances car, selon l'a.
2563 C
.c., une faute intentionnelle
de l'assuré n'est pas couverte par le contrat d'assurance... Selon cette
jurisprudence, qui n'est cependant pas très claire, la faute intentionnelle
c'est bien sûr une faute commise avec la volonté déterminée de causer le dommage
qui est arrivé, mais c'est aussi une faute lourde dolosive. Or cette notion est
plus délicate à préciser, car elle se distingue de la faute lourde simple, qui
elle n'est pas considérée comme intentionnelle. La distinction entre les deux
relève en fait des circonstances propres à chaque espèce, car dans les deux
cas, l'auteur de la faute n'a pas véritablement voulu commettre les
conséquences de son acte, qui témoigne cependant dans les deux cas d'une
insouciance grave à l'égard de la vie ou de la sécurité d'autrui. La différence
réside dans le degré de cette insouciance, par rapport au caractère immédiat ou
inéluctable des conséquences qu'il connaissait et qui ne l'ont pas empêché
d'agir quand même. One insouciance déréglée et téméraire de la sécurité d'autrui
constituera une faute dolosive, assimilable à une faute intentionnelle, car
l'auteur a agi avec la conscience des conséquences immédiates de son acte qui
ne manqueraient pas de se réaliser. Il les a sues à l'avance et a cependant
agi, ce qui témoigne d'une conscience malicieuse ou malveillante révèlent (sic)
un état d'âme dolosif, c'est-à-dire marqué du signe de la mauvaise foi. Si au
contraire, l'insouciance est moins grave. parce que le risque de la réalisation
des conséquences était moins immédiat, car il s'agissait plutôt d'une
éventualité, il s'agira d'une faute lourde, mais non dolosive et, en
conséquence, d'un acte non assimilable à une faute intentionnelle. Il s'agit en
fait pour les tribunaux de déterminer dans chaque cas, d'après les circonstances
de l'espèce, si l'on se situe à la limite du volontaire ou de l'involontaire.
Faute lourde simple et faute lourde dolosive se séparent par l'intention
malicieuse.

Si l'on applique cette notion de faute intentionnelle à l'
a. 49
al.
2 de la
Charte
, qui utilise ce concept,
les dommages et intérêts punitifs ne
seront accordée que dans le cas de faute intentionnelle ou de faute lourde
dolosive, ils ne le seront pas dans le cas d'une faute lourde simple
..."

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

This Court is satisfied that gross
negligence ("faute lourde") is not sufficient to trigger liability
for exemplary damages under the second paragraph of
s. 49
, as the law of Québec
exists today
(
[17]
)
. However, to insist upon proof of the defendant's
subjective

intent to breach the victim's
Québec Charter
rights would practically
emasculate the second paragraph of
s. 49
and most violators would escape
condemnation. It would appear that the proper place on the continuum to locate
the degree of fault necessary to trigger exemplary damages would be as close as
possible to wanton or reckless misconduct ("faute lourde dolosive")
(
[18]
)
.

The reasoning of Nichols J. in
Potvin

v.
Stipetic
(
[19]
)
, although specifically referring to "faute légère" and
"faute lourde", are equally applicable with respect to "faute
lourde dolosive" :

"...La ligne de démarcation
entre la faute légère, la faute moyenne et la faute lourde reste floue, et
chaque cas doit s'apprécier en fonction des circonstances.

Celles-ci varieront selon le genre
d'activité, l'époque, le lieu, la qualité des personnes et que sais-je encore."

In the present case : the type
of activity is the handling of a deadly weapon and not a carpenter's
tool : the time is 1987 and not 1887 in the Wild West ; the place is a
police station parking lot in broad daylight not an alleyway in the slums in
the dark of the night and the person involved is an experienced police officer
and not a novice handling a gun for the first time.

The fact that Constable Gosset's
revolver fired when handled by him in the mariner he did was an eminently
foreseeable development and one which he ought to have known to be a serious
danger to Anthony's personal security. In the Court's opinion, it is not
necessary for Plaintiff and Intervenant to show that Constable Gosset subjectively
assumed the risk involved and deliberately acted on the face of this risk. The
very nature of the act of pointing at Anthony a loaded revolver, held in one
hand with the finger on the trigger, at almost point-blank range clearly
demonstrates a wanton and reckless disregard for the life of Anthony (and
others who might have been in the line of fire). The necessary intention can be
inferred from the act itself. Therefore, it is the Court's opinion that
Constable Gosset's actions were an unlawful and intentional interference with
Anthony's rights under the first paragraph of
s. 1
of the
Québec Charter
.

VICARIOUS LIABILITY OF MUC FOR
EXEMPLARY DAMAGES

Plaintiff and Intervenant argue that
the MUC is vicariously liable under the last paragraph of Art. 1054 C.C. for
any exemplary damages to which Constable Cosset may be condemned. This point
does not yet appear to have been addressed directly by a Québec court.

In
Halkett
v.
Ascofigex
Inc.
(
[20]
)
, a sexual harassment case under
s. 10.1
of the
Québec Charter
, the
court condemned the employee and employer jointly and severally to pay $1,300
material damages, $2,000 moral damages and $2,000 exemplary damages. The court
made no distinction between the compensatory and exemplary damages when it
condemned the employer under Art. 1054 C.C. It simply based itself on a commentary by Me Madeleine Caron
(
[21]
)
on a recently issued court decision.
However, a careful reading of the decision and of Me Caron's article shows that
they both dealt with moral damages and not exemplary damages.

In
Commission des droits de la
personne du Québec
v.
La Compagnie Bombardier M.L.W. Ltée
(
[22]
)
, a racial discrimination case, the
court did not find the employee responsible and therefore the employer could
not be vicariously liable.

However, in certain obiter remarks,
the court did suggest that an employer should not be condemned under the last
paragraph of Art. 1054 C.C. for
the breach by its employee of rights under
ss. 10
to
19
and
48
of the
Québec
Charter
.

It has been suggested that the
remarks of La Forêt J. in the unanimous decision of the Supreme Court of
Canada,
Robichaud
v.
Canada (Treasury Board)
(
[23]
)
, dealing with a matter of sexual
harassment under the
Canada Human Rights Act
(
[24]
)
, is authority for upholding the
doctrine of vicarious liability in human rights legislation. However, as
Dickson C.J. pointed out in a subsequent decision,
Janzen
v.
Platy
Enterprise Ltd
(
[25]
)
, La Forêt J. had
not tried to apply principles of vicarious liability, saying that this was
unhelpful and unnecessary since the employer's liability could be found within
the statute itself.

It is elementary that a parent or a
master can be found vicariously liable for the compensatory damages caused by
the fault of a child or of a servant in the performance of the work for which
the servant was employed. However, generally speaking, the vicarious imposition
of exemplary damages is extremely suspect since it runs contrary to fundamental
moral principles against vicarious punishment. Mosaic law (Deuteronomy 24:16)
provides that ;

"The fathers shall not he put
to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the
fathers. Every man shall he put to death for his own sin."

It has often been stated that the
"scope of employment" rule encourages employers to exercise greater
care in selecting, training and supervising their employees. However, this
rationale has validity only to the extent that the employer has sufficient
behaviour control over the employee to warrant holding the former responsible
for the latter's acts. Human behaviour is notoriously difficult to predict and
control, especially the type of behaviour that leads to exemplary damages.

Another criticism of the employer
diligence rationale is that the existence of liability insurance weakens it
considerably by permitting an employer to shift the burden of exemplary damages
to an insurer. Although public policy militates against allowing the actual
wrongdoer to insure against his own intentional act, there is a strong body of
U.S. jurisprudence to the effect that an employer can insure against exemplary
damages which are vicariously imposed
(
[26]
)
. These decisions reason that public
policy is not offended by allowing insurance coverage for the employer since
the employer is not the actual wrongdoer and therefore deserves no punishment.

Finally, when the employer is a
government agency or organism, vicarious liability for exemplary damages would
only serve to punish innocent citizens whose taxes would be raised or services
cut back to make up for the award.

In the case of a breach of the
Québec
Charter
right to personal security and inviolability, the Court is of the
opinion that an employer should not be vicariously liable for exemplary damages

unless the employer has expressly or implicitly authorized or ratified the
employee's reprehensible act
. It should be emphasized that authorization
should extend not only to the
performance
of the act but also to the
manner

purportedly authorized.

Ratification differs from
authorization in that it involves approval
after
the reprehensible
conduct of the employee. Ratification can be implied from the employer's
actions or inaction. For example, it could be inferred where an employer fails
to discipline or dismiss an employee after he has committed the wrongful act.
However, failure to dismiss an employee will not always be sufficient to
establish ratification. For example, an employer might retain the employee not
out of an intent to ratify his wrongful act but simply because the employee was
a loyal and faithful servant for many years. Care must obviously be taken not
to infer ratification from acts not necessarily indicative of it.

It is true that the MUC is paying
the legal expenses of Constable Gosset for his defense in the present matter.
However, the MUC is doing so in virtue of its contractual obligations under
Art. 26.00 of the collective labour agreement between it and La Fraternité des
policiers de la Communauté
urbaine de Montréal Inc. (Exhibit C-125) and a legal opinion the MUC received
concerning the interpretation of the provisions of the said agreement.

The Court is satisfied that the MUC
did not authorize Constable Gosset to use the kind of force he did to try and
bring Anthony into Station 15. Furthermore, the fact that the MUC immediately
suspended and subsequently dismissed him at a police officer indicates there
was no ratification of Constable Gosset's actions. Finally, the MUC contested
(but to no avail) his request to be reinstated as a police officer. Therefore,
the MUC is not vicariously liable for any exemplary damages Constable Gosset
may be condemned to pay.

COMPENSATORY DAMAGES

The award for compensatory damages
under Arts 1053 and 1056 C.C. must be fair to both Plaintiff and Intervenant as
well as to Constable Gosset. The ability to pay has never been regarded as a
relevant consideration in the assessment of this type of damages. However, such
consideration is relevant in the calculation of exemplary damages. The
assessment of compensatory damages must be neither punitive nor influenced by
sentimentality. It is largely an exercise of business judgment
(
[27]
)
.

a
Funeral Expenses

It is now settled law that because
funeral expenses are a charge on the estate of the deceased (Art. 2002 C.C.), the near relatives specified in
Art. 1056 C.C. may only recover these expenses if they show that they had to
pay them because there were not sufficient funds in the estate
(
[28]
)
. The funeral expenses for Anthony
were admitted at $3,591. It was also admitted that his estate was insolvent. As
Plaintiff and Intervenant agreed that the funeral expenses should be divided
equally between them, the Court grants to each of them for this item the sum of
$1,795.50.

b.
Loss of Life Expectancy

The claim of the victim of a delict
or quasi-delict for damages suffered during his lifetime passes to his heirs.
However, the claim for shortening of life or loss of life expectancy cannot be
included because
it is caused by the death
(
[29]
)
, i.e., it was not felt by the victim
while he was alive. No amount is awarded by the Court for this item.

c.
Pain, and Suffering

To support a claim by the heirs for
the pain and suffering of the deceased, it must be shown that the suffering
was, in fact, felt by the victim
while alive
(
[30]
)
. If the victims dies without
regaining consciousness, nothing will be awarded under this item. The medical
and pathological proof in the present case is quite clear to the effect that
Anthony lost consciousness immediately following the shooting and fell deeper
and deeper into a coma until he expired about four hours after his injury. The
fact that his pain reflex may still have been functioning for a few minutes
after the shooting does not indicate that Anthony was consciously aware of his
injuries. Therefore, nothing is awarded for this item,

d.
Solatium Doloris

In claims by parents under Art. 1056 C.C., Québec courts have consistently
refused to award damages for the injured feelings, the anguish and the mental
suffering of the parents. They are not entitled to recover damages in respect
of and by way of consolation for the bereavement they have suffered
(
[31]
)
.

The philosophical basis for the
courts refusal to entertain a claim of this nature is most poignantly expressed
by the words of Deslauriers J.
(
[32]
)
:

"... Le tribunal tient en
effet qu'il n'y a pas lieu en droit d'accorder une indemnité pour les larmes
d'une mère, ni pour les soupirs d'un père à la suite de la mort de son enfant.
Le chagrin, les regrets, les larmes et les soupirs ne sont, en effet, dans
l'opinion du tribunal, qu'indirectement liés à l'accident mortel. C'est à
l'occasion de l'accident, il est vrai, que ces réactions se manifestent à des
degrés divers d'intensité. Mais elles sont déterminées immédiatement par la
constatation ou la réalisation plus ou moins complète et réfléchie de la perte
subie par la mort. Elles sont un effet secondaire dans le résultat de
l'accident. Qu'il s'agisse de la perte d'un mari, d'un enfant ou d'un père ou
d'une mère, les larmes versées à cette occasion et les déchirements ressentis
ne durent qu'un temps. Les unes se tarissent, les autres se cicatrisent plus ou
moins rapidement, Les douleurs s'atténuent et la mémoire s'en efface. Les
larmes se contrôlent, le chagrin se raisonne. Ces manifestations sont
subjectives et varient à l'infini. Tel qui parait terrassé sous le coup de la
plus violente affliction, est touché moins profondément qu'un autre qui endure
sa douleur muettement avec un stoïcisme et une force morale héroïque. La nature
humaine est ainsi faite que le temps estompe le souvenir des plus cruelles
épreuves."

Therefore, nothing is awarded for
this item.

e.
Loss of Future Support

Because of the grossly exaggerated
amounts claimed by Plaintiff and Intervenant in the present case, and because
of the American jurisprudence on quantum submitted by Plaintiff's attorney, the
Court feels obliged to cite the words of Lesage J. in
Maheux
v.
Lavallée
(
[33]
)
:

"... La Cour d'appel,
cependant, nous met en garde contre l'octroi de sommes trop élevées. L'avocat
des demandeurs a plaidé avec vigueur que le temps est révolu d'accorder pour le
décès d'enfants sur le point d'être majeurs, des sommes qu'il a qualifiées de
ridiculement basses. Il faut cependant appliquer la loi telle qu'elle est. Ce
serait rendre un bien mauvais service aux plaideurs que de se laisser
impressionner par les décisions américaines pour voir ensuite leur cause
frappée d'un appel sérieux, qui leur ferait perdre en frais ce qui pourrait
être considéré comme une indemnité raisonnable."

The following is a brief summary of
recent Québec jurisprudence concerning claims by parents for the death of a
son :

-
Bergeron
v.
Gagnon
-Ellefsen
(
[34]
)
:

Son aged 20 - Eldest of five children
- Mature young man with sense of family responsibility - Lived with his widowed
mother and other children - Just completed first year of university with
excellent marks - Had worked every summer since age 15 - Contributed
financially to support of the family.

MOTHER RECEIVED $10,000.

-
Gagnon
v.
Breton
(
[35]
)
:

Son aged about 30 - Unmarried - Second
Youngest of 6 children - Mechanic earning around $30,000 per annum - Lived with
his father (61) and his mother (53) who were not working - Contributed $9,000 a
year to their support.

EACH PARENT RECEIVED $7,000.

-
Picard
v.
Gravel
(
[36]
)
:

Son aged 34 - Unmarried - Oldest of 4
children - Lived with his parents - Earned about $35,000 per annum -
Contributed money to his parents so they could travel - Close-knit family.

EACH PARENT RECEIVED $12,500.

-
Gaudet
v.
Roger
Baudin Automobiles Inc.
(
[37]
)
:

Son aged 18 - Eldest of 4 children‑
Apprentice mechanic for last year - Lived with his parents - Contributed $20 a
week to family expenses - Father died during litigation.

MOTHER RECEIVED $10,000.

-
Lévesque
v.
Dubé
(
[38]
)
:

Son aged 22 - Oldest of 5 children -
Had just obtained his B.Sc. from McGill University ‑ Lived with his parents
Close family relationship - Father not in need of support.

EACH PARENT RECEIVED $7,000.

-
Guilbeault
v.
Blais
(
[39]
)
:

Son aged 17 and daughter aged 16 -
Both killed in same accident - The only two children of their parents - Both

Finally, in the 1982 case of
Bulger

v.
Up-Right Aluminum Scaffolds Ltd
(
[40]
)
, concerning the death of a 16-year
old daughter, the Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of the trial judge
reducing the civil jury award (in the days when civil juries existed in Québec)
of $25,000 to each parent to the sum of $5,000 for each parent. Jacques J.
opined that the sum of $25,000 awarded by the jury to each parent was
unreasonable. His colleague, Paré J., pointed out that the sum of $25,000 was
five times the amount permitted by recent Québec jurisprudence in similar
situations.

When considering prior awards for
the loss of a son, the Court may also take judicial notice of the fact that a
general inflationary trend exists
(
[41]
)
.

The award of damages is not simply
an exercise in mathematics which a judge indulges in, leading to a
"correct" global figure. The evidence of actuaries can be of value in
arriving at a fair and just result. However, the judge who is required to make
the decision must be accorded a large measure of freedom in dealing with the
evidence presented by the experts. If the figures of the experts lead to an
award which in all the circumstances seems to the judge to be inordinately
high, it is his duty to adjust these figures downward. In like manner, they
should be adjusted upward if they lead to what seems to be an unusually low
award.

There is always the possibility of
incapacity to earn occasioned by industrial or other accident or illness. There
should be added to that contingency the possibility that the victim, had he
lived, might have been unable to provide support to his dependents for a
variety of other reasons - some emotional, some mental, some due to later-developed
changes in character. In short, the future of any individual is filled with
unforeseen events and the possibility of their occurring must be considered as
a contingency in awarding damages for death and injury
(
[42]
)
.

The Court must consider whether
there is any evidence which takes the deceased's situation outside the
"average", i.e., whether there are any features of which no account
was taken in actuarial tables, either because the factor is entirely personal
to the individual or because the "average" is not adapted for the
category or class to which the deceased belongs
(
[43]
)
.

Anthony was Plaintiff's only
surviving child. Up until he left home in January 1986 (at age 17 and against
Plaintiff's wishes), the proof indicates that Anthony was a good-looking, shy,
quiet, polite and loving young man in excellent health. Anthony's father
abandoned him and Plaintiff when Anthony was two years of age. However,
Plaintiff did her beet to support and educate Anthony. It was only after
Anthony left home that things began to go downhill for him.

Anthony dropped out of high school
in March 1986 and never graduated. One has only to look at his marks for the
Years 1984, 1985 and 1986 to realize that he was a poor student. Furthermore,
he was often guilty of poor effort and disruptive behaviour in class.

Anthony would not tell his mother
where he was living although he did telephone her from time to time. The last
time Plaintiff saw Anthony before his death was in March 1987.

After he left school, there is
nothing in the proof to indicate that he held down a job for any significant
period of time. There is no proof that he ever contributed any money to
Plaintiff's or Intervenant's support.

Both Plaintiff and Intervenant
admitted that Anthony had fallen in with bad company. Other than mentioning his
prior imprisonment for breaking and entering and that at the time of his arrest
he was wanted on a bench warrant for another pending charge of breaking and
entering, it is not necessary to dwell at length on Anthony's continuing problems
with the law. However, he appears to have been heading for serious trouble in
the near future.

The facts of this case indicate that
Anthony would probably have had difficulty in earning sufficient money to
support himself without taking on the added burden of contributing to the
support of his parents.

Luckily for Plaintiff, who is
presently 47 years of age, the probability of her requiring support from him in
the future is relatively remote. In 1977 she married her present husband. Both
of them have good jobs and are each earning approximately $30,000 per annum.
They own their own home valued at approximately $100,000 and they expect to pay
off the last few thousand dollars of mortgage this Year.

Intervenant, presently 48 years of
age, abandoned Plaintiff and Anthony in August 1970 to live and work in New York. Between 1972 and 1985. Intervenant
had no contact whatsoever with Anthony. Apart from a few hundred dollars sent
to Plaintiff in the year following their separation, he never made any further
attempt to contribute to Anthony's support (or to that of Plaintiff).

A decree absolute of divorce between
Plaintiff and Intervenant was rendered May 23, 1975.

Intervenant has three other children
born of three different mothers. In February of this year he married the woman
who bore his son, Adrian, presently aged 12, He contributes to the support of
his other two children, two daughters aged 5 and 9 respectively.

Intervenant is self-employed in
Brooklyn, New York as a heavy
equipment mechanic earning approximately $50,000 U.S. gross per annum. His new wife, aged 45, earns approximately $26,000
U.S. per annum. Other than his
1984 Lincoln Continental automobile and $5,000 in the bank. Intervenant
possesses no other property. He also testified that he would like to work as
long as possible,

When asked why he had made no
attempt to visit Anthony for more than 14 years, he replied "I expected
when he gets older, somehow he would find me". In fact, it was Anthony who
took the initiative and visited his father twice in New
York, once for a few months in 1986 and again for a
few days in 1987. Things did not work out and Anthony returned to Montréal.
Intervenant's suggestion that Anthony would eventually work with him in his
business is, in the Court's opinion, pure speculation with no basis in fact.

Furthermore, the Court is of the
opinion that Anthony would not voluntarily have contributed to his father's
support in the future. Luckily. Intervenant has a good job, a new wife and
three children he can look to if he is ever really in need,

The reports and testimony of the two
actuaries are of little help to the Court. This is because the Court has come
to the conclusion that Anthony would probably have been unable to contribute
any percentage of his income to support his parents. Therefore, the assumptions
upon which the actuarial proof was based were incorrect.

However, the death of a child
involves a very real loss that goes considerably beyond the narrow question of
future financial support. In
Pearce
v.
Buckley
(
[44]
)
, Deslauriers J. described the nature
of such a loss :

"Les parents qui perdent un
enfant ne sont pas seulement frappés dans leurs sentiments. Ils perdent un
actif qui a son prix. Les enfants pour un père et une mère sont un de leurs
buts principaux dans la réalisation duquel ils mettent le plus de labeurs.
Quand par la faute d'un chauffeur imprudent ils sont privée de leur enfant, ils
sont gravement et injustement frustrés. Ils subissent un tort réel, Les enfante
n'existent pas simplement pour donner éventuellement quelques dollars à des
vieux parents. Bien souvent, ceux-ci n'ont pas besoin de cette aide.

L'avantage pour les parents
d'avoir des enfants a, sur toute leur vie, une influence considérable. Pour le
père, ils peuvent motiver l'ambition et l'ardeur au travail qui lui permettra
de donner la pleine mesure de ses talents. Chez la mère, les mêmes réactions se
manifestent sous des formes différentes.

À part le secours pécuniaire que
peut apporter un enfant, son existence rend possible une infinité de services ou
d'agréments utiles dont les parents sont privés par le décès. La liste peut en
être longue. C'est son aide à entretenir la maison lorsqu'il se trouve, comme
dans le présent cas que le père est propriétaire de sa demeure ; ce sont
des vacances partagées, des séjours pour les parents plus ou moins prolongés
chez leur enfant, des voyages en commun, des prêts sans intérêts, des cadeaux
en toutes sortes de circonstances, à l'occasion des fêtes, d'anniversaires de
naissances, d'anniversaires de mariages, etc. Même éloignés, l'existence des
enfants a sur la vie des parents une influence bienfaisante indéniable. Quand
les enfants et les petits-enfants sont là, il est moins difficile pour les
parents de vieillir."

The Court, after carefully
considering the rather special facts of this case, has determined that
Plaintiff should receive the sum of $9,000 for the lose of her son, which sum
includes the loss of moral support and the lose of any possible material
support. With respect to Intervenant, the Court feels that the sum of $2,000 is
quite reasonable under the circumstances.

nor the
