EXEMPLARY DAMAGES UNDER S. 49 OF
QUEBEC
CHARTER

a.
General

The concepts of exemplary damages
and punitive damages are English common law concepts which, historically, were
unknown to the law of Québec
(
[45]
)
. Damages used to be awarded to the
victim of an offence or a quasi offence for the sole purpose of compensating
him for the harm done. In recent years, however, several statutes providing for
the remedy of exemplary damages have been enacted by the Québec legislature,
including the
Québec Charter
.

The object of exemplary damages is
not to compensate the victim for the harm he has suffered. Exemplary damages
have a different purpose. They are intended to deter the wrongdoer, and others
who might be tempted to imitate his reprehensible behaviour, from repeating
this kind of conduct
(
[46]
)
.

It is to be noted that the Quebec legislature chose the term
"exemplary damages" rather than the term "punitive
damages". In the opinion of the Court, the word "exemplary"
better expresses
the policy
of the law, This policy is intended to teach
the defendant and others that certain reprehensible conduct does not pay by
demonstrating what consequences the law inflicts, The word
"punitive", on the other hand, connotes punishment which more
properly belongs to the domain of criminal law, "Punitive" implies
that the defendant should suffer an extra punishment for what he has done.
Punishment does, however, describe one of
the effect
of exemplary
damages.

Plaintiff's attorney submitted many
American court decisions on the question of punitive damages for racial
discrimination in police forces in American cities. Québec courts must be
careful in using these cases as precedents. As Gonthier J. (then a member of
the Superior Court) pointed out
(
[47]
)
:

"... Le droit américain nous
offre l'expérience la plus longue et la plus riche. Elle est d'un secours
certain et une ressource précieuse. Il faut pourtant se garder de penser que
ses solutions sont nécessairement indiquées ou même valables chez nous. La
grande parenté de nos institutions et de nos sociétés ne doit pas nous faire
oublier d'importantes divergences. Les interprétations américaines sont
marquées par le texte de leur Constitution, son histoire et l'évolution de
cette société et de la jurisprudence de ses tribunaux. Le Canada n'a pas connu
l'esclavage, la guerre civile, ni la philosophie du "melting pot"
fruit d'une croissance très rapide. L'évolution de nos fédéralismes n'est pas
la même..."

b.
Transmissibility of Right to
Claim Exemplary Damages

Life is the most precious possession
of any person. Without it, there is nothing earthly for such a person. Wealth,
influence, position and power all vanish when it expires. Throughout the world,
people fight for life daily with all their force. The first paragraph of
s. 1

of the
Québec Charter
recognizes this most fundamental of all rights. Without
life, all other rights of an individual become meaningless.

The
Québec Charter
is silent on
whether the right to claim for breach of
s. 1
survives the death of the victim.
However, if the second paragraph of s. 49 does not allow recovery of exemplary
damages by the estate of a victim who died as a result of a breach of rights
under
s. 1
, would not the very purpose of the second paragraph of 49 be
subverted ? It would be more advantageous for the wrongdoer to let his
victim die. It would seem anomalous to hold that Anthony could have sought
exemplary damages for violation of his
s. 1
rights had he survived Constable
Gosset's unlawful actions but, because these actions caused his death, the law
is impotent to require application of one of the very sanctions provided by s.
49. Surely this cannot be the intent of this public and fundamental law as it
exists today.

To say that the right of action for
exemplary damages dies with the victim seems to fly in the face of certain of
the basic purposes one finds in the preamble to the
Québec Charter
, namely to
foster "respect for the dignity of the human being" and to ensure
that fundamental human rights will be "better protected against any
violation",

When a law is doubtful or ambiguous,
it is to be interpreted so as to fulfil the intention of the legislature, and
to attain the object for which it was passed
(
[48]
)
.

The doctrine of exemplary damages
originated in the English courts in the middle of the eighteenth century
(
[49]
)
. It continued to develop
jurisprudentially for the next 170 years without statutory interference. It was
only in 1934 that the British Parliament adopted a Law Reform (Miscellaneous
Provisions) Act that provided in s. 1 (2) (a) that the damages in an action for
the benefit of an estate "shall not include any exemplary damages".

In the common law provinces of Canada the incidence of exemplary damages
in survival actions is largely governed by statute. In Alberta, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, it is expressly
declared that a claim for exemplary damages shall not survive for the benefit
of the estate. However, this Statutory amputation of a part of the right to
claim exemplary damages has been the subject of universal criticism in England and Canada
(
[50]
)
.

The general thrust of the criticism
is to the effect that wherever exemplary damages are awarded to a living
plaintiff, they cannot be justified on a compensatory basis. So, if enrichment
of a living plaintiff is tolerable, presumably in the public interest, so also
should be enrichment of his estate. On the other hand, if enrichment of the
estate seems anomalous, that must lead the observer to question the whole basis
of exemplary damages.

It is up to the courts of Québec
(unless the Legislature decides to intervene) to integrate the doctrine of exemplary
damages with existing civil law concepts and rules. In this respect, the first
paragraph of Art. 596 C.C. states :

"Succession is the transmission by law or by the will of man,
to one or more persons, of the property and the
transmissible rights
and
obligations of a deceased person."

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

Anthony, who had no brothers or
sisters, died intestate. His sole heirs are his mother and his father
(
[51]
)
.

Art. 607 C.C. provides that : "
The
lawful heirs, when they inherit, are seized by, law alone of the property,
rights and actions of the, deceased
..." One starts with the premise
that the generality of Art. 607 C.C., couched as it is in the widest terms, is
restricted only when one finds the victim in possession of rights of action which
by their very nature are incapable of being transmitted. The only rights of
action not transmitted under Art. 607 are the ones which cannot possibly
survive the person who possessed or enjoyed them
(
[52]
)
.

Inasmuch as Québec courts permit the
transmission by death of the right to claim
moral
damages, the Court has
great difficulty in understanding why the right to claim exemplary damages
should not also be transmissible. The lucid and logical words of Professor
Mayrand
(
[53]
)
(as he then was) concerning the transmissibility of the right to
claim moral damages are, in the opinion of this Court, equally applicable to
the right to claim exemplary damages :

"Comme aucun texte ne laisse
entendre que le droit à des dommages moraux et causés la personne est
intransmissible, il ne reste plus qu'à voir si ce droit ne serait pas
intransmissible de par sa nature. Les droits intransmissibles par nature
n'étant définis nulle part, on a cru devoir les assimiler aux droits
exclusivement attachés à la personne dont il est question à l'art.
1031 C
. C. Dans l'arrêt sous étude,
le juge Casey condamne cette façon de voir. Les créanciers d'une personne
blessée ne peuvent réclamer les dommages subis par leur débiteur, mais il ne
s'ensuit pas que les héritiers de la victime sont soumis à la même règle.
Mignault explique qu'il y a entre la victime et ses héritiers une solidarité
d'honneur qui n'existe point entre elle et ses créanciers.

Les droits attachés à la personne
ne sont intransmissibles qu'à la condition d'être en plus extrapatrimoniaux.
Or, tous ne le sont pas, par exemple, le droit à une indemnité pour douleurs
endurées et pour abrégement de la vie.
Car la destruction par la faute d'un
tiers d'un bien extrapatrimonial, tel que l'intégrité physique ou la vie, fait
naître un droit à une indemnité, à une somme d'argent et ce droit est
manifestement patrimonial dès sa naissance, avant même d'avoir été réclamé en
justice. Le fait juridique qui métamorphose le bien extrapatrimonial en bien
patrimonial, ce n'est pas la signification de l'action qui a donné naissance au
droit d'action. Quant au jugement qui alloue les dommages, il est, à ce point
de vue, simplement déclaratif
.

On ne doute pas que ce droit fasse partie du patrimoine de
l'accidenté durant sa vie. Pourquoi son décès le ferait-il disparaître ?
Les règles de la transmission successorale ne varient pas selon l'origine des
biens. Une fois qu'il a pris naissance, le droit à une somme d'argent, quelle
qu'en soit la cause juridique, passe à l'héritier continuateur de la personne
du de cujus."

(underlining
by the undersigned)

Not only is the right to claim
exemplary damages capable by its "very nature" of being transmitted
but, by its "very nature", it
should
be transmitted, to the
heirs of a deceased victim.

The following remarks of Owen J. in
Lévesque

v.
Malinosky
(
[54]
)
, although made in the context of
claims for pain and suffering and for shortening of life, are equally
applicable to a claim for exemplary damages :

When we come to items such as pain
and suffering, shortening of life and loss of enjoyment of life there is a
strong body of opinion that such items are not transmissible. Why ? It is
difficult to prove the amount of these items. It is said that they represent
damage
à la personne
or
extra-patrimonial
or for
préjudice
moral
as opposed to damage
aux biens
or
patrimonial
or for a
préjudice
matériel
. There is certainly a difference between these items and the items
previously considered. However, each of these items can be expressed in terms
of money and if they are not collected they represent an impoverishment of the
estate of the de cujus.

(...)

... the best practical solution is
to lay down the general rule that the right which the de cujus had prior to his
death to claim damages resulting from an offence or quasi-offence, including
all items which are properly part of such claims, is transmissible in toto by
succession. "

Anthony's right to claim exemplary
damages was born the moment Constable Cosset unlawfully and intentionally
pointed his revolver at him. At the same moment was born Constable Gosset's
obligation to pay exemplary damages, conditional of course on the future and
uncertain event of such damages being awarded by the Court. Although Constable
Gosset's conditional obligation results from the sole and direct operation of
the law, the Court can see no reason why Art. 1085 C.C. concerning conditional
obligations created by contract, should not be applied by analogy :

"1085. The fulfilment of the condition has a retroactive effect
from the day on which the obligation has been contracted.
If the creditor be
dead before the fulfilment of the condition, his rights pass to his heirs or
legal representatives
."

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

c.
Quantum of Exemplary Damaged

The
Québec Charter
gives no hint as
to the manner in which the amount of exemplary damages should be calculated.
The determination of the correct figure cannot be made in a precise scientific
or actuarial manner
(
[55]
)
.

The Court suggests that the
following criteria can be applied to the calculation of the amount of exemplary
damages flowing from the breach of a person's right to personal security and
inviolability under
s. 1
of the
Québec Charter
:

1
The deterrent and preventive
role such damages play
, The award must be such that it is meaningful and
effective. It must reflect the deterrent aspect for which exemplary damages are
awarded. The amount should be substantial so that others will know it is not
profitable to engage in similar conduct.

2.
The conduct of the defendant
.
The subsequent sorrow or apology of the defendant should not exclude the
possibility of an award of exemplary damages. To permit an apology to wipe out
exemplary damages would make it too easy for insincere defendants to escape
punishment.

3.
The seriousness of the
prejudice suffered by the victim
.

4.
The financial resources of the
defendant
. A relatively small award could still bring hardship to a poor
man. However, it would require a substantial sum to punish properly a wealthy
individual or a large corporation.

5.
The amount of compensatory
damages awarded to the victim
.

6.
The duration of the
reprehensible conduct of the defendant
. Conduct of this nature that was
repeated or lasted over a long period of time should warrant a higher award
than conduct that lasted only for a few minutes.

7.
Any Punishment Already meted
out to the defendant
by a criminal court, a professional disciplinary body
or a regulatory agency, or for contempt of court proceedings, and pertaining to
the same reprehensible conduct.

8.
The amount of any profit or
benefit derived by the defendant from his reprehensible behaviour
. To be an
effective deterrent, the award must make it unprofitable to violate another's
rights. To assess exemplary damages at a small figure would amount only to a
licence fee.

9.
Any provocation on the part of
the victim
. If the victim provoked the defendant into harming him he may be
denied exemplary damages. However, provocation should not prevent the award if
the defendant's response so greatly exceeds the provocation that a wanton and
reckless assault results.

The first five of these criteria
have recently been approved by the Court of Appeal
(
[56]
)
.

Applying these criteria to the
present case, the Court notes that Constable Gosset's conduct in the parking
lot, although it lasted only a matter of seconds, was an inexcusable
infringement of Anthony's right to personal security and inviolability. It
resulted in the most serious prejudice possible - death.

Although Anthony's attempt to flee
was. in a certain sense, provocation, under no circumstances did this warrant
such excessive use of force by Constable Gosset.

Constable Gosset, apart from his
salary of $47,000 per annum and his pension fund, has no other income or assets
of importance. He derived no benefit or profit from this unfortunate incident.

As far as prior punishment is
concerned, Constable Cosset was suspended from the police force the same day of
the shooting. He was subsequently dismissed on July 8, 1988, Following the
filing of a grievance by his union, he was reinstated as a police officer on
August 24, 1989. This reinstatement was confirmed by the Superior Court on
November 2, 1989 following a petition in evocation. He has received no salary
for the period between his suspension and his reinstatement.

He was charged with manslaughter and
was acquitted, The Crown has appealed his acquittal and the appeal is pending.

Constable Gosset's attorney
suggested during argument that until the criminal proceedings against his
client have finally terminated. this Court has no right to consider an award of
exemplary damages against him. The Court does not agree with this reasoning.
The criminal and civil courts are capable of functioning in parallel and one
court need not await the judgment of the other court
(
[57]
)
. Just as the civil courts can
consider a prior penal sanction as a mitigating factor in determining the
amount of exemplary damages to be awarded, the judge called upon to sentence in
the criminal court can consider a prior civil award of exemplary damages as a
mitigating circumstance.

It is interesting to note that the
$7,000 exemplary damages awarded by the trial court to the torture victim in
Papadatos

v.
Sutherland
(
[58]
)
was eliminated by the Court of
Appeal on the grounds that the defendant had already been sentenced to
imprisonment for ten years, and further punishment by way of exemplary damages
was not required. Rothman J. opined that at p. 1022 :

"...
Article 49
of the
Quebec
Charter was not intended to
permit a court, in a civil action, to award exemplary or punitive damages where
the Defendant has already been prosecuted and punished for the same acts in the
criminal courts."

This Court is of the opinion that
prior punishment in virtue of a penal statute should not
automatically

exclude an amount of exemplary damages under the
Québec Charter
but could be a
mitigating factor in the calculation of the amount of such damages. Rothman J.
implicitly seems to accept. this point of view when he says further on in the
Papadatos

judgment
(
[59]
)
:

"... there may (sic) cases
where the sanctions imposed under penal statutes are inadequate to punish and
deter a wrong-doer for deliberate violations of the
Charter
. In these cases,
the awarding of exemplary damages way be appropriate."

What amounts of exemplary damages
have Québec courts awarded for the unlawful and intentional interference with
the right to personal security and inviolability ? In
Sutherland
v.

Papadatos
(
[60]
)
, the trial judge awarded $7,000 for seven hours of physical
aggression, torture and humiliation.

In
Tevan
v.
Hôtel Bord du
Lac/Lakeshore Hotel Inc.
(
[61]
)
, a bar and discotheque patron was
granted $11,095 of compensatory damages and $3,000 of exemplary damages after
being physically dragged through the club and thrown out the door by two
doormen employed by the hotel.

In
Falardeau
v.
Duchesneau
(
[62]
)
, the victim was awarded $507 of
compensatory damages and $500 of exemplary damages when defendant threatened
the victim with physical force during a confrontation between neighbours over a
country property.

In
Gagnon
v.
Landry
(
[63]
)
a hockey coach, who was attacked in
the team locker-room after a game by a member of the opposing team, received
$15,000 for skull fracture, facial scar and permanent partial incapacity and
$1,000 for exemplary damages.

In
Gaudreault
v.
Drapeau
(
[64]
)
the victim, who was having domestic
problems with her spouse, was attacked by her in-laws causing her superficial
facial scars, bruises and emotional shock. She received $7,813 for compensatory
damages and $500 of exemplary damages.

After considering all relevant
criteria and prior jurisprudence, the Court concludes that an award of $8,000
of exemplary damages is reasonable in the circumstances of the present case. It
should be noted, however, that this amount would have been considerably higher
had Constable Gosset not been suspended and dismissed by the MUC with the
consequent loss of salary.

Because these exemplary damages are
not "damages occasioned by the death" of the victim, the Court does
not have the discretion it enjoys under Art. 1056 C.C. to determine what proportion of
the exemplary damages should go to Plaintiff and what proportion should go to Intervenant.
In virtue of Art. 626 C.C., Plaintiff and Intervenant share the exemplary
damages equally, i.e., $4,000 for each of them.

d.
Interest and Additional
indemnity under Art. 1056 (c) C.C.

On the question of interest and the
additional indemnity under Art. 1056 (c) C.C. on exemplary damages, the Court
shares the opinion recently expressed by Baudoin J.
(
[65]
)
:

"La créance de l'obligation
de compenser le préjudice illégitimement causé à autrui existe dès le moment où
les trois éléments constitutifs de la responsabilité (faute, dommage, lien de
causalité) sont établis. Le législateur aurait donc pu faire courir l'intérêt
dès ce moment. Il a préféré fixer celui-ci à l'assignation. C'est, en effet, à
ce moment que l'auteur du délit sait de façon claire et officielle le montant
auquel la victime prétend avoir droit. Le premier peut donc, dès lors,
acquiescer à jugement en totalité ou en partie et arrêter le loyer de l'argent
de la créance. La situation me parait différente lorsqu'il s'agit de dommages
exemplaires. Tout d'abord, ils ne sont pas dus à titre de compensation pour une
perte subie ou un gain manqué, mais bien comme sanction. Ensuite, leur octroi
reste exceptionnel, ne touchant que les cas particuliers prévus par la loi et
avec les restrictions imposées par celle-ci. De plus, et surtout, ils sont
abandonnés à la discrétion du juge quant à leur attribution ("le tribunal
peut")...

Il me semble, en effet, pour les raisons mentionnées plus haut, que
les
intérêts et l'indemnité supplémentaire
qui, de toute façon, malgré son nom,
est reconnue comme étant une sorte d'intérêt supplémentaire sur les dommages
punitifs
ne devraient commencer à courir que de la date du jugement de
première instance
. Il y a lieu de les imposer cependant dés ce moment pour
forcer la partie condamnée à acquitter sa dette immédiatement et à ne pas se
livrer à des manœuvres dilatoires."

(Underlining
by the undersigned)

COSTS
.

BY her Amended Declaration,
Plaintiff is seeking a special fee of $150,000 "...  pursuant to the
provisions of Rule R-14 of the Bar Act, 1966-67, C. 77". Presumably what
Plaintiff's attorney is referring to, is really Art, 15 of the
Tarif des
honoraires judiciaires des avocats
(
[66]
)
:

The Court may, upon request or
ex
officio
, grant a special fee, in addition to all other fees, in an
important case."

During argument, Plaintiff's
attorney admitted that $150,000 was perhaps somewhat high and that $60,000
would probably be a more reasonable sum !

The sole explanation for this
request is contained in paragraph 43 of the Amended Declaration :

"...the present case,
pertaining to Plaintiff's desire to invoke her rights under the
Quebec Charter
of Human Rights and Freedoms
, as well as the right by Plaintiff in seeking
pursuant to
Section 24
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, has
required :

i)          numerous witnesses ;

ii)         numerous
inquiries ;

iii)         numerous
meetings with witnesses ;

iv)        extensive
research in numerous jurisdictions to assemble the relevant
jurisprudence ;

and as a consequence thereof,
Plaintiff is seeking that the Court grant a special fee in partial payment and
in addition to the taxable Bill of Costs, to contribute toward the cost of
prosecuting her rights before this Honourable Court ;".

Apart from this paragraph 43,
Plaintiff's attorney made no effort to suggest to the Court which of the
objective factors and criteria normally referred to by the courts for
determining, the importance of the case
(
[67]
)
would be applicable.

At first glance, one would think
that a proof which took 22 days to complete, the testimony of 70 witnesses and
the filing of 169 exhibits would denote an "important" case. However,
the testimony of the majority of the witnesses was often irrelevant to the
issues before the Court and unnecessarily repetitive on certain facts. With
respect to the exhibits filed by Plaintiff's attorney, less than one third of
them were necessary and relevant (and some were even contrary to Plaintiff's
own interests).

It should also be remembered that
responsibility for the compensatory damages was admitted by the MUG.

There was very little technical
proof and the one expert witness, an actuary, produced by Plaintiff's attorney
was of little use in advancing Plaintiff's interests or enlightening the Court.

As a result of the Québec Police
Commission inquiry, the criminal trial, the arbitration hearing and the
subsequent evocation trial, most of the relevant facts were known in advance by
Plaintiff's attorney as was the testimony of most of the witnesses he called.

The Court is well aware that it must
not take into consideration the experience, skill or reputation of the attorney
requesting the additional fee
(
[68]
)
. However, the Court is of the
opinion that it does have the right to consider the manner in which such
attorney presented the proof and conducted himself during the trial.

Attorneys for Defendants argued
vehemently that Plaintiff's attorney should be condemned personally to pay part
of the taxable costs of this trial.

With respect to the 22 days required
by Plaintiff's attorney to make his proof, the Court notes that :

(1)       he was late in arriving for 12
different sittings of the Court ;

(2)       he presented a motion to amend
Plaintiff's Declaration in the middle of the trial, which motion was completely
unnecessary ;

(3)       he objected to the filing of the
transcript of prior testimony of a ballistics expert (at which testimony he had
been present) and later, in argument, thanked the Court for dismissing his
objection ;

(4)       after signing an admission to avoid
the attendance of a subpoenaed witness, he then reissued a subpoena to the same
witness thereby provoking unnecessary argument during an entire sitting ;
and

(5)       when Intervenant's attorney (a sole
practitioner) was obliged to represent another client in an urgent criminal
matter on June 4, 1990, Plaintiff's attorney argued against a one day
postponement of the present matter.

Taxable costs are supposed to be
compensatory in nature and not punitive
(
[69]
)
. The special fee authorized by Art.
15 of the Tarif is not intended to take the place of extra-judicial fees.

Considering the manner in which
Plaintiff's attorney chose to conduct his client's case, an award of a special
fee would only serve to punish Defendants unduly in the circumstances of this
particular matter, Therefore, Plaintiff's request for a special fee is refused.

Finally, the costs to which
Defendants will be condemned will be limited to a total of 12 days of proof and
hearing.

FOR THE ABOVE REASONS, THE
COURT :

CONDEMNS
Defendant, Allan Gosset to pay to Plaintiff exemplary damages in the
amount of $4,000, with interest and the additional indemnity provided for under

CONDEMNS
Defendant Allan Gosset to pay to Intervenant exemplary damages in
the amount of $4,000, with interest and the additional indemnity provided for

CONDEMNS
Defendants jointly and severally to pay to Plaintiff compensatory
damages in the amount of $10,795, with interest and the additional indemnity
provided for under Art. 1056 (c) C.0 from the date of service of the
action ; the whole with costs based on a Class III-A action under the Tarif,
but which costs are limited to twelve (12) days of proof and hearing ;

CONDEMNS
Defendants Jointly and severally to pay to Intervenant compensatory
damages in the amount of $3,795, with interest and the additional indemnity
provided for by Art. 1056 (c) C.C., from the date the Intervention was
received ; the whole with costs based on a Class Il-B action under the Tarif,
but which costs are limited to 12 (12) days of proof and hearing ;

DISMISSES
Plaintiff's request for a special fee under Art. 15 of the
Tarif des honoraires judiciaires des avocats
